lines: -type: library-entry
-kind: case-study
-domain: strength-and-conditioning
-book: block-periodization--issurin
-chapter: "4.4.3"
-topic: retrospective performance benchmarking for talent identification
-category: [case-study, talent-identification, retrospective-analysis]
-confidence: untested
-ingest-tier: full-text
-# 35 Elite Soviet Paddlers: What Age-14-15 Performance Looked Like Before They Were Elite
-**What it is** — Issurin cites a retrospective interview study of 35 "world leading
-canoe-kayak paddlers who took part in the USSR National team and earned medals in
-the Olympic Games and World Championships within eight years prior to the study"
-(PDF p. 163, printed p. 152, citing Sozin, 1986). Respondents were interviewed about
-their official performance results from ages 14-15, "the end of their first year of
-long-term preparation"; athletes who began preparation later were excluded from the
-analysis. "The collected data were subjected to statistical analysis and the
-performance trends of elite paddlers were calculated" (PDF p. 163, printed p. 152); no
-statistics are reported. Figure 4.10 (PDF p. 163, printed p. 152; page image) plots
-performance time on a 500-m course by one-year age step (14-15, 15-16, 16-17, 17-18,
-18-19) for three groups: at 14-15, kayak males about 139 s, kayak females about 146 s,
-canoeists about 151 s; at 18-19, about 101.5 s, 118.5 s and 119 s. Kayak males are
-fastest at every step, and kayak females and canoeists track close together. The
-figure runs to 18-19 although the interview was about official results "from ages
-14-15"; the book does not say where the later points come from. The book frames the
-result as
-a usable historical benchmark rather than a fixed standard: "despite the substantial
-improvement of paddles and boats in the two decades since this study was conducted,
-the results achieved by outstanding athletes in the earlier stages of their preparation
-remain relevant to this day for evaluation of giftedness in today's young athletes" (PDF
-p. 163, printed p. 152).
-**Why it works** — **The author gives no mechanism** connecting age-14-15
-performance time to eventual elite status; the case is presented purely as a descriptive
-benchmark curve, not as a validated predictive model. The book says the data were
-"subjected to statistical analysis" but reports no correlation, sensitivity, or
-false-positive/false-negative rate for using these times to screen today's youngsters. Issurin's own claim that equipment-era changes do not invalidate
-the benchmark is asserted, not tested against any comparison of era-adjusted times.
-**When to apply** — The book files this case under "retrospective studies, in which
-the development of outstanding athletes is carefully analyzed with respect to
-performance trend, changes in body size etc." (PDF p. 162, printed p. 151), an approach
-it presents separately from the longitudinal and cross-sectional "model
-characteristics" of Bulgakova (1986)
-([[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]]). **Inference:** as a
-template, not as transferable numbers, interviewing an already-elite cohort about their
-own performance at a fixed early-career age point, to build a reference curve for
-today's youngsters, is a reusable talent-identification method independent of the
-specific canoe-kayak times.
-**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is a retrospective,
-survivorship-selected sample: all 35 respondents were already-successful medalists at
-the time of interview. Inference: the study therefore cannot say what fraction of
-14-15-year-olds with similar performance times failed to reach the same level (no
-comparison group of similarly-fast 14-15-year-olds who did not become elite). It is also
-sport- and era-specific (Soviet canoe-kayak, single national federation, with the book
-noting "substantial improvement of paddles and boats in the two decades since this
-study was conducted"; Inference: the medals fall in roughly the late 1970s to
-mid-1980s, given the 1986 citation and the "within eight years prior to the study"
-window) with no cited data from any other sport or country, and the book's
-own claim that "the results... remain relevant to this day" is the author's assertion, not
-a re-tested comparison against a current cohort. Do not use the specific second-count
-benchmarks as a screening cutoff for any current sport without independent
-verification.
-**Example** — **Inference:** the method (not the numbers) could be adapted for a
-sport Applied Performance evaluates by asking current or recent elite alumni for their
-own testing numbers at a fixed early developmental checkpoint (e.g. end of a true
-freshman year), building an internal reference curve for how "what elite eventually
-looked like at this checkpoint" compares to a current prospect, while explicitly
-tracking that such a curve, built only from athletes who succeeded, cannot say how
-many similarly-scoring peers did not.
-**Related** — [[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]],
-[[heuristic--dual-approach-initial-level-and-improvement-rate-giftedness]],
-[[case-study--troup-swimmers-maturation-timing-and-longevity]].

-category: [youth, talent-identification, ltad]

-# Four Talent Factors, Graded by How Fixed They Are
-**What it is** — Issurin defines giftedness as "a predisposition to and a higher
-trainability for a given activity," treated as "genetically transmitted properties of an
-individual," such that "a gifted child is potentially a talented athlete" (PDF p. 160,
-printed p. 149). Citing Williams & Franks (1998) and Williams & Reilly (2000), he
-organizes talent prediction into four factors, each graded by genetic determination
-(Table 4.11, PDF p. 161, printed p. 150; **verified against the page image**):
-**Body build and body composition**: body height, extremity length, foot size
-(strong); shoulder width, thigh circumference, muscle mass (medium); total body fat
-(low). **Physiological**: alactic anaerobic power, peak blood lactate, space
-orientation (high); glycolytic anaerobic power, strength endurance/acidity resistance,
-flexibility (medium). **Psychological**: self-confidence, anxiety control, motivation,
-concentration (medium-low), citing Plomin et al. (1994) and Saudino (1997) for a
-partial heritable component. **Sociological**: parental support, socio-economic
-background, cultural background, coach-child interaction (heredity independent,
-though the text adds: "this doesn't mean, however, that they can be changed easily if
-necessary"). Psychological traits are "somewhat inherited (Plomin et al., 1994;
-Saudino, 1997) and therefore can be altered during preparation" (PDF p. 160, printed p.
-149). Issurin's practical point in presenting the table this way: "some
-anthropometrical and physiological variables are highly dependent on heredity and as
-such, can not be compensated for by other personal traits. Thus, they can restrict
-progress in a given sport" (PDF p. 160, printed p. 149). Inference: the high-heritability
-rows work as constraints on which sports an athlete can realistically excel in, while the
-lower-heritability rows are more open to training and environment; the book itself
-warns that heredity-independent sociological factors are not necessarily easy to change.
-The book gives no numeric heritability estimates; Table 4.11 grades each factor only
-qualitatively (strong, medium, low, high, medium-low, heredity independent).
-The unchangeable-predictor approach is operationalized through "model
-characteristics" (Bulgakova, 1986; PDF p. 161, printed p. 150): favorable
-anthropometric/physiological combinations by age category, built from longitudinal
-study of a large athlete group where a sub-group reaches elite level (citing Vorontsov
-et al. 1999 and Falk et al. 2003 as examples of this being done despite its difficulty),
-or more commonly from cross-sectional studies comparing less- and more-successful
-youngsters (PDF p. 162, printed p. 151). Issurin flags the model characteristics' central
-limitation directly: "the main limitation of this evaluation is in the differing levels of
-maturity of children that are examined to determine giftedness. Children with slower
-rates of maturation may be found inferior to more mature teammates but may have
-greater potential for further progress" (PDF p. 161, printed p. 150). Genetic
-contribution to training response itself is not constant across a career: "Based on the
-outcomes of studies with young adult twins, it has been found that the contribution of
-heredity related factors to training response in an endurance program is different for
-earlier and later stages of preparation. The initial preparation is less dependent on
-heredity. However, as athletes progress and approach higher workloads, the genetic
-control of their training response becomes much stronger (Bouchard et al., 2000)."
-The book adds that this "partly explains why some gifted endurance athletes cannot be
-effectively recognized at an earlier stage of their preparation" (PDF p. 167, printed p.
-156). The book cites these twin studies via Bouchard, Wolfarth, Rivera et al. (2000),
-"Genetic determinants of endurance performance," a review chapter in *Endurance in
-Sport*, Vol. II of the Encyclopedia of Sports Medicine (reference list, PDF p. 169,
-printed p. 158); the primary twin studies are not named in the book and were not
-checked here.
-**Why it works** — The heredity-grading in Table 4.11 is presented without a
-citation for individual cells (the surrounding text cites Williams & Franks 1998 and
-Williams & Reilly 2000 for the four-factor taxonomy); it functions as the author's
-synthesized taxonomy rather than a reported finding with its own effect sizes. The
-genetic-control claim is cited to a review chapter (Bouchard et al., 2000), not to a
-primary twin study.
-**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly relevant to how Applied Performance and
-recruiting staff frame "traits we can develop" versus "traits we are selecting for":
-Table 4.11's strong/medium/low-heritability split is a usable lens for separating
-recruiting criteria (anthropometrics, alactic power, space orientation: closer to fixed)
-from developmental targets (glycolytic capacity, strength endurance, flexibility,
-psychological skills: more trainable), while the maturation-confound caution is a
-direct argument for tracking training age and biological maturation alongside any
-"talent" read on a young or first-year athlete, consistent with
-[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]].
-**When NOT to apply** — The cited taxonomy sources are soccer talent-ID papers
-(Williams & Franks 1998, "Talent identification in soccer"; Williams & Reilly 2000,
-"Talent identification and development in soccer"; reference list, PDF p. 170, printed
-p. 159); the chapter's own examples are swimming, canoe-kayak and gymnastics.
-**Inference, population caveat:** American football's position-specific demands are
-not addressed, and no cell in Table 4.11 is football-specific. The heritability labels ("strong," "medium," "high," "medium-low") are
-qualitative and unsourced at the individual-cell level in this passage; treat them as the
-author's organizing synthesis, not as quantified heritability estimates. The
-maturation-confound caution applies most directly to youth/pre-collegiate evaluation
-and is less relevant once an athlete has finished growth, though the same caution about
-mistaking current-training-age effects for fixed talent still applies to a true freshman.
-**Example** — **Inference:** using the four-factor split as a talking-point framework
-when a coach asks whether a trait is coachable: anthropometrics and alactic power
-profile are closer to "select for, don't expect to build"; strength endurance,
-flexibility, and psychological-skill factors are closer to "build through training and
-sport psychology support," while sociological factors (family support, coach-athlete
-relationship) sit entirely outside a strength staff's typical intervention but are named
-here as real contributors to development that the book says are heredity independent
-but not necessarily easy to change.
-**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--speed-barrier-is-genetic-ceiling-not-neural-block]],
-[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]],
-[[heuristic--dual-approach-initial-level-and-improvement-rate-giftedness]],
-[[case-study--troup-swimmers-maturation-timing-and-longevity]],
-[[framework--long-term-preparation-four-stage-model-and-directions]] (the book's
-counterweight: lower-fitness children may catch up during preliminary preparation).

+necessary"). Psychological traits are "somewhat inherited (Plomin et al., 1994;
+Saudino, 1997) and therefore can be altered during preparation" (PDF p. 160, printed p.
+149). Issurin's practical point in presenting the table this way: "some
+anthropometrical and physiological variables are highly dependent on heredity and as
+such, can not be compensated for by other personal traits. Thus, they can restrict
+progress in a given sport" (PDF p. 160, printed p. 149). Inference: the high-heritability
+rows work as constraints on which sports an athlete can realistically excel in, while the
+lower-heritability rows are more open to training and environment; the book itself
+warns that heredity-independent sociological factors are not necessarily easy to change.
+The book gives no numeric heritability estimates; Table 4.11 grades each factor only
+qualitatively (strong, medium, low, high, medium-low, heredity independent).
+The unchangeable-predictor approach is operationalized through "model
+characteristics" (Bulgakova, 1986; PDF p. 161, printed p. 150): favorable
+anthropometric/physiological combinations by age category, built from longitudinal
+study of a large athlete group where a sub-group reaches elite level (citing Vorontsov
+et al. 1999 and Falk et al. 2003 as examples of this being done despite its difficulty),
+or more commonly from cross-sectional studies comparing less- and more-successful
+youngsters (PDF p. 162, printed p. 151). Issurin flags the model characteristics' central
+limitation directly: "the main limitation of this evaluation is in the differing levels of
+maturity of children that are examined to determine giftedness. Children with slower
+rates of maturation may be found inferior to more mature teammates but may have
+greater potential for further progress" (PDF p. 161, printed p. 150). Genetic
+contribution to training response itself is not constant across a career: "Based on the
+outcomes of studies with young adult twins, it has been found that the contribution of
+heredity related factors to training response in an endurance program is different for
+earlier and later stages of preparation. The initial preparation is less dependent on
+heredity. However, as athletes progress and approach higher workloads, the genetic
+control of their training response becomes much stronger (Bouchard et al., 2000)."
+The book adds that this "partly explains why some gifted endurance athletes cannot be
+effectively recognized at an earlier stage of their preparation" (PDF p. 167, printed p.
+156). The book cites these twin studies via Bouchard, Wolfarth, Rivera et al. (2000),
+"Genetic determinants of endurance performance," a review chapter in *Endurance in
+Sport*, Vol. II of the Encyclopedia of Sports Medicine (reference list, PDF p. 169,
+printed p. 158); the primary twin studies are not named in the book and were not
+checked here.
+**Why it works** — The heredity-grading in Table 4.11 is presented without a
+citation for individual cells (the surrounding text cites Williams & Franks 1998 and
+Williams & Reilly 2000 for the four-factor taxonomy). Inference: it functions as the
+author's synthesized taxonomy rather than a reported finding with its own effect sizes. The
+genetic-control claim is cited to a review chapter (Bouchard et al., 2000), not to a
+primary twin study.
+**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly relevant to how Applied Performance and
+recruiting staff frame "traits we can develop" versus "traits we are selecting for":
+Table 4.11's strong/medium/low-heritability split is a usable lens for separating
+recruiting criteria (anthropometrics, alactic power, space orientation: closer to fixed)
+from developmental targets (glycolytic capacity, strength endurance, flexibility,
+psychological skills: more trainable), while the maturation-confound caution is a
+direct argument for tracking training age and biological maturation alongside any
+"talent" read on a young or first-year athlete, consistent with
+[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]].
+**When NOT to apply** — The cited taxonomy sources are soccer talent-ID papers
+(Williams & Franks 1998, "Talent identification in soccer"; Williams & Reilly 2000,
+"Talent identification and development in soccer"; reference list, PDF p. 170, printed
+p. 159); the chapter's own examples are swimming, canoe-kayak and gymnastics.
+**Inference, population caveat:** American football's position-specific demands are
+not addressed, and no cell in Table 4.11 is football-specific. The heritability labels ("strong," "medium," "high," "medium-low") are
+qualitative and unsourced at the individual-cell level in this passage; treat them as the
+author's organizing synthesis, not as quantified heritability estimates. The
+maturation-confound caution applies most directly to youth/pre-collegiate evaluation
+and is less relevant once an athlete has finished growth, though the same caution about
+mistaking current-training-age effects for fixed talent still applies to a true freshman.
+**Example** — **Inference:** using the four-factor split as a talking-point framework
+when a coach asks whether a trait is coachable: anthropometrics and alactic power
+profile are closer to "select for, don't expect to build"; strength endurance,
+flexibility, and psychological-skill factors are closer to "build through training and
+sport psychology support," while sociological factors (family support, coach-athlete
+relationship) sit entirely outside a strength staff's typical intervention but are named
+here as real contributors to development that the book says are heredity independent
+but not necessarily easy to change.
+**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--speed-barrier-is-genetic-ceiling-not-neural-block]],
+[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]],
+[[heuristic--dual-approach-initial-level-and-improvement-rate-giftedness]],
+[[case-study--troup-swimmers-maturation-timing-and-longevity]],

Read first, fully: WT\docs\ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md, WT\AGENTS.md (conventions), WT\docs\method-baseline.md (for any "Eric's baseline:" line: it must match this file, quote its wording; the review flags a false "Eric's baseline:" line in this batch), then the round-1 review WT\staging\review_supertraining_ch4-2b_opus.md.

Task: apply EVERY FIX row (and every batch-wide problem it lists) of that review to the 20 files listed in WT\staging\_scope_supertraining_ch4-2b.txt, which live in WT\staging\library\strength-and-conditioning\supertraining--verkhoshansky\ . Open every cited page and figure yourself from WT\staging\books\supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf before writing any number or figure description: entries cite the 0-based PDF page = printed page + 11; the Read tool's PDF viewer page is 0-based + 1 (so Read pages "229" shows 0-based 228). You may also render pages with PyMuPDF (python, fitz) to PNG in your temp dir and Read the PNG, zooming crops for figures. Do not trust the review blindly: if the page contradicts the review's correction, follow the page and note it in your log. The review says two more entries may deserve `contested` (regime choice, quad:hamstring ratio): decide from the pages under the brief's rule and log why. Missing ideas: do NOT write new entries.

Write ownership: you may edit ONLY the 20 scoped files, plus _book.md in that folder ONLY if the review asks for a change there (another fixer works on 15 other files in the same folder concurrently; never touch files outside your scope), and create/write WT\staging\fixes_supertraining_ch4-2b_applied.md. No git. No vault edits (C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain is read-only; you may grep it to confirm links resolve).

Rules: labels "Eric's baseline:" (must match method-baseline.md), "Eric's review:", "Inference:", "External:". Plain text = the authors' statements only (Supertraining is Siff and Verkhoshansky: write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one; a passage naming Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff). Unsourced mechanisms/examples get "Inference:". Record source contradictions both ways with pages and set `contested` where the brief says so. Reviewer "(verify)" citations (e.g. Gregory and Bickel 2005, Wilke 1999, Ward and Shkuratova 2002) come from memory: NEVER insert one unless you confirm it in the vault or the paper itself; otherwise leave it out and say so in the log. Section headers exactly "**What it is** —" (and the other five in the same form, with the em dash); no em dashes in titles or body text; never wrap a [[wikilink]] across lines; no review history in entries ("prior version", "corrected", "round 1" etc. belong only in the log). Every number carries a PDF page (and printed page).

Log format in fixes_supertraining_ch4-2b_applied.md: a table `| file | what changed |`, one row per file (say "no change needed" with reason where applicable), then "Disagreements with the review", "Reciprocal-link suggestions" (other-book or vault entries that should link back to these entries, with the exact line to add), and "Checks" where you paste the actual output of: `cd WT && PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 python scripts/lint_library.py staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky` (known false positives: _book.md title/table dashes; issues in files outside your scope are someone else's) and your own grep for em dashes and review-history words over the 20 files. The log must match the files exactly.

Final reply: a short summary (counts of files changed, contested decisions, disagreements, anything you could not verify).

"""Append reciprocal Related links from a staging/reciprocal_links_*.md table to vault files.

    python scripts/apply_reciprocal_links.py staging/reciprocal_links_2026-09-27.md           # dry run
    python scripts/apply_reciprocal_links.py staging/reciprocal_links_2026-09-27.md --apply

Run AFTER promote_to_vault.py --apply, so every source file is in the vault. Table rows:
| source (path under Knowledge/library, domain optional) | [[target]] | location | text | origin |
Library entries: the text is added as a new line at the end of the **Related** paragraph, or
a **Related** paragraph is created at the end of the file. Paper briefs: added as a bullet
under "## Related knowledge" (replacing a "None identified" placeholder). A row is skipped
when the source already links the target.
"""
import argparse
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

VAULT = Path(r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library")


def resolve(src: str) -> Path | None:
    src = src.strip().strip("`")
    hits = [p for p in VAULT.rglob("*.md") if p.as_posix().endswith("/" + src)]
    return hits[0] if len(hits) == 1 else None


def add(text: str, line: str) -> str:
    lines = text.rstrip("\n").split("\n")
    if "## Related knowledge" in text:
        i = next(k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("## Related knowledge"))
        j = i + 1
        while j < len(lines) and not lines[j].startswith("## "):
            j += 1
        block = [l for l in lines[i + 1:j] if l.strip() and "None identified" not in l]
        if block and not block[-1].startswith("- "):
            block.append("")
        return "\n".join(lines[:i + 1] + [""] + block + [f"- {line}", ""] + lines[j:]).rstrip("\n") + "\n"
    rel = [k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("**Related**")]
    if rel:
        j = rel[-1] + 1

-# 35 Elite Soviet Paddlers: What Age-14-15 Performance Looked Like Before They Were Elite
-**What it is** — Issurin cites a retrospective interview study of 35 "world leading
-canoe-kayak paddlers who took part in the USSR National team and earned medals in
-the Olympic Games and World Championships within eight years prior to the study"
-(PDF p. 163, printed p. 152, citing Sozin, 1986). Respondents were interviewed about
-their official performance results from ages 14-15, "the end of their first year of
-long-term preparation"; athletes who began preparation later were excluded from the
-analysis. "The collected data were subjected to statistical analysis and the
-performance trends of elite paddlers were calculated" (PDF p. 163, printed p. 152); no
-statistics are reported. Figure 4.10 (PDF p. 163, printed p. 152; page image) plots
-performance time on a 500-m course by one-year age step (14-15, 15-16, 16-17, 17-18,
-18-19) for three groups: at 14-15, kayak males about 139 s, kayak females about 146 s,
-canoeists about 151 s; at 18-19, about 101.5 s, 118.5 s and 119 s. Kayak males are
-fastest at every step, and kayak females and canoeists track close together. The
-figure runs to 18-19 although the interview was about official results "from ages
-14-15"; the book does not say where the later points come from. The book says the
-results "remain relevant to this day": "despite the substantial
-improvement of paddles and boats in the two decades since this study was conducted,
-the results achieved by outstanding athletes in the earlier stages of their preparation
-remain relevant to this day for evaluation of giftedness in today's young athletes" (PDF
-p. 163, printed p. 152).
-**Why it works** — **The author gives no mechanism** connecting age-14-15
-performance time to eventual elite status; the case is presented purely as a descriptive
-benchmark curve, not as a validated predictive model. The book says the data were
-"subjected to statistical analysis" but reports no correlation, sensitivity, or
-false-positive/false-negative rate for using these times to screen today's youngsters. Issurin's own claim that equipment-era changes do not invalidate
-the benchmark is asserted, not tested against any comparison of era-adjusted times.
-**When to apply** — The book files this case under "retrospective studies, in which
-the development of outstanding athletes is carefully analyzed with respect to
-performance trend, changes in body size etc." (PDF p. 162, printed p. 151), an approach
-it presents separately from the longitudinal and cross-sectional "model
-characteristics" of Bulgakova (1986)
-([[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]]). **Inference:** as a
-template, not as transferable numbers, interviewing an already-elite cohort about their
-own performance at a fixed early-career age point, to build a reference curve for
-today's youngsters, is a reusable talent-identification method independent of the
-specific canoe-kayak times.
-**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is a retrospective,
-survivorship-selected sample: all 35 respondents were already-successful medalists at
-the time of interview. Inference: the study therefore cannot say what fraction of
-14-15-year-olds with similar performance times failed to reach the same level (no
-comparison group of similarly-fast 14-15-year-olds who did not become elite). It is also
-sport- and era-specific (Soviet canoe-kayak, single national federation, with the book
-noting "substantial improvement of paddles and boats in the two decades since this
-study was conducted"; Inference: the medals fall in roughly the late 1970s to
-mid-1980s, given the 1986 citation and the "within eight years prior to the study"
-window) with no cited data from any other sport or country, and the book's
-own claim that "the results... remain relevant to this day" is the author's assertion, not
-a re-tested comparison against a current cohort. Do not use the specific second-count
-benchmarks as a screening cutoff for any current sport without independent
-verification.
-**Example** — **Inference:** the method (not the numbers) could be adapted for a
-sport Applied Performance evaluates by asking current or recent elite alumni for their
-own testing numbers at a fixed early developmental checkpoint (e.g. end of a true
-freshman year), building an internal reference curve for how "what elite eventually
-looked like at this checkpoint" compares to a current prospect, while explicitly
-tracking that such a curve, built only from athletes who succeeded, cannot say how
-many similarly-scoring peers did not.
-**Related** — [[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]],
-[[heuristic--dual-approach-initial-level-and-improvement-rate-giftedness]],
-[[case-study--troup-swimmers-maturation-timing-and-longevity]].

-# Four Talent Factors, Graded by How Fixed They Are
-**What it is** — Issurin defines giftedness as "a predisposition to and a higher
-trainability for a given activity," treated as "genetically transmitted properties of an
-individual," such that "a gifted child is potentially a talented athlete" (PDF p. 160,
-printed p. 149). Citing Williams & Franks (1998) and Williams & Reilly (2000), he
-organizes talent prediction into four factors, each graded by genetic determination
-(Table 4.11, PDF p. 161, printed p. 150; **verified against the page image**):
-**Body build and body composition**: body height, extremity length, foot size
-(strong); shoulder width, thigh circumference, muscle mass (medium); total body fat
-(low). **Physiological**: alactic anaerobic power, peak blood lactate, space
-orientation (high); glycolytic anaerobic power, strength endurance/acidity resistance,
-flexibility (medium). **Psychological**: self-confidence, anxiety control, motivation,
-concentration (medium-low), citing Plomin et al. (1994) and Saudino (1997) for a
-partial heritable component. **Sociological**: parental support, socio-economic
-background, cultural background, coach-child interaction (heredity independent,
-though the text adds: "this doesn't mean, however, that they can be changed easily if
-necessary"). Psychological traits are "somewhat inherited (Plomin et al., 1994;
-Saudino, 1997) and therefore can be altered during preparation" (PDF p. 160, printed p.
-149). Issurin's practical point in presenting the table this way: "some
-anthropometrical and physiological variables are highly dependent on heredity and as
-such, can not be compensated for by other personal traits. Thus, they can restrict
-progress in a given sport" (PDF p. 160, printed p. 149). Inference: the high-heritability
-rows work as constraints on which sports an athlete can realistically excel in, while the
-lower-heritability rows are more open to training and environment; the book itself
-warns that heredity-independent sociological factors are not necessarily easy to change.
-The book gives no numeric heritability estimates; Table 4.11 grades each factor only
-qualitatively (strong, medium, low, high, medium-low, heredity independent).
-The unchangeable-predictor approach is operationalized through "model
-characteristics" (Bulgakova, 1986; PDF p. 161, printed p. 150): favorable
-anthropometric/physiological combinations by age category, built from longitudinal
-study of a large athlete group where a sub-group reaches elite level (citing Vorontsov
-et al. 1999 and Falk et al. 2003 as examples of this being done despite its difficulty),
-or more commonly from cross-sectional studies comparing less- and more-successful
-youngsters (PDF p. 162, printed p. 151). Issurin flags the model characteristics' central
-limitation directly: "the main limitation of this evaluation is in the differing levels of
-maturity of children that are examined to determine giftedness. Children with slower
-rates of maturation may be found inferior to more mature teammates but may have
-greater potential for further progress" (PDF p. 161, printed p. 150). Genetic
-contribution to training response itself is not constant across a career: "Based on the
-outcomes of studies with young adult twins, it has been found that the contribution of
-heredity related factors to training response in an endurance program is different for
-earlier and later stages of preparation. The initial preparation is less dependent on
-heredity. However, as athletes progress and approach higher workloads, the genetic
-control of their training response becomes much stronger (Bouchard et al., 2000)."
-The book adds that this "partly explains why some gifted endurance athletes cannot be
-effectively recognized at an earlier stage of their preparation" (PDF p. 167, printed p.
-156). The book cites these twin studies via Bouchard, Wolfarth, Rivera et al. (2000),
-"Genetic determinants of endurance performance," a review chapter in *Endurance in
-Sport*, Vol. II of the Encyclopedia of Sports Medicine (reference list, PDF p. 169,
-printed p. 158); the primary twin studies are not named in the book and were not
-checked here.
-**Why it works** — The heredity-grading in Table 4.11 is presented without a
-citation for individual cells (the surrounding text cites Williams & Franks 1998 and
-Williams & Reilly 2000 for the four-factor taxonomy). Inference: it functions as the
-author's synthesized taxonomy rather than a reported finding with its own effect sizes. The
-genetic-control claim is cited to a review chapter (Bouchard et al., 2000), not to a
-primary twin study.
-**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly relevant to how Applied Performance and
-recruiting staff frame "traits we can develop" versus "traits we are selecting for":
-Table 4.11's strong/medium/low-heritability split is a usable lens for separating
-recruiting criteria (anthropometrics, alactic power, space orientation: closer to fixed)
-from developmental targets (glycolytic capacity, strength endurance, flexibility,
-psychological skills: more trainable), while the maturation-confound caution is a
-direct argument for tracking training age and biological maturation alongside any
-"talent" read on a young or first-year athlete, consistent with
-[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]].
-**When NOT to apply** — The cited taxonomy sources are soccer talent-ID papers
-(Williams & Franks 1998, "Talent identification in soccer"; Williams & Reilly 2000,
-"Talent identification and development in soccer"; reference list, PDF p. 170, printed
-p. 159); the chapter's own examples are swimming, canoe-kayak and gymnastics.
-**Inference, population caveat:** American football's position-specific demands are
-not addressed, and no cell in Table 4.11 is football-specific. The heritability labels ("strong," "medium," "high," "medium-low") are
-qualitative and unsourced at the individual-cell level in this passage; treat them as the
-author's organizing synthesis, not as quantified heritability estimates. The
-maturation-confound caution applies most directly to youth/pre-collegiate evaluation
-and is less relevant once an athlete has finished growth, though the same caution about
-mistaking current-training-age effects for fixed talent still applies to a true freshman.
-**Example** — **Inference:** using the four-factor split as a talking-point framework
-when a coach asks whether a trait is coachable: anthropometrics and alactic power
-profile are closer to "select for, don't expect to build"; strength endurance,
-flexibility, and psychological-skill factors are closer to "build through training and
-sport psychology support," while sociological factors (family support, coach-athlete
-relationship) sit entirely outside a strength staff's typical intervention but are named
-here as real contributors to development that the book says are heredity independent
-but not necessarily easy to change.
-**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--speed-barrier-is-genetic-ceiling-not-neural-block]],
-[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]],
-[[heuristic--dual-approach-initial-level-and-improvement-rate-giftedness]],
-[[case-study--troup-swimmers-maturation-timing-and-longevity]],
-[[framework--long-term-preparation-four-stage-model-and-directions]] (the book's
-counterweight: lower-fitness children may catch up during preliminary preparation).

import re, sys, pathlib

rev_path, folder = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]), pathlib.Path(sys.argv[2])
dry = "--dry" in sys.argv
rev = rev_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").replace("\r\n", "\n")
body = rev.split("## Exact corrections", 1)[1]
body = re.split(r"\n## (?!#)", body)[0]
secs = re.split(r"\n(?=\*\*C\d+)", body)
pair = re.compile(
    r"(?:C\d+[a-z] )?Old:\s*\n```[a-z]*\n(.*?)\n```\s*\n(?:C\d+[a-z] )?New:\s*\n```[a-z]*\n(.*?)\n```"
    r"|Old: `(.+?)`\s*\nNew: `(.+?)`",
    re.S,
)
ok = bad = 0
for s in secs:
    m = re.match(r"\*\*(C\d+)[^`]*`([^`]+)`", s)
    if not m:
        continue
    tag, fname = m.group(1), m.group(2)
    p = folder / fname
    if not p.exists():
        print(tag, "MISSING FILE", fname); bad += 1; continue
    raw = p.read_bytes().decode("utf-8")
    crlf = "\r\n" in raw
    t = raw.replace("\r\n", "\n")
    pairs = pair.findall(s)
    if not pairs:
        print(tag, fname, "NO PAIRS PARSED"); bad += 1; continue
    for a, b, c, d, e, f in pairs:
        o, n = (a, b) if a or b else ((c, d) if c or d else (e, f))
        cnt = t.count(o)
        print(tag, fname, "hits", cnt)
        if cnt == 1:
            t = t.replace(o, n); ok += 1
        else:
            bad += 1
    if not dry:
        p.write_bytes((t.replace("\n", "\r\n") if crlf else t).encode("utf-8"))
print("applied", ok, "failed", bad)

# Handoff 2026-09-28: Flint day 3

Read `docs/STATUS.md` first. This covers the gate work on the day-2 ingest wave. All four batches now pass the gate. **Nothing has been written to the vault yet**: the promotion is ready to run as one command and is waiting for Eric.

## Done (all on branch `step1-triage`, pushed)

| Batch | Entries | Round 2 (independent reviewer) | Corrections applied | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Issurin Ch4 | 10 | done on day 2 (GO AFTER FIXES) | 3 required + 2 optional edits, verbatim (`257a3ef`) | **passes** |
| Zatsiorsky 2e Ch1-2 | 17 | `staging/review_zatsiorsky_ch1-2_opus_round2.md`: 14 FIXED, 2 GO (the 2 new entries), 2 NEW PROBLEM, 0 STILL FIX | C1-C8 (2 required, 6 optional), log in `fixes_zatsiorsky_ch1-2_applied.md` | **passes** |
| *Supertraining* 4.1 | 6 | passed on day 2 | none | **passes** |
| *Supertraining* 4.2a (4.2 intro, 4.2.1-4.2.3) | 15 | round-1 fixes by a separate fixer, then `review_supertraining_ch4-2a_opus_round2.md`: 2 GO, 11 NEW PROBLEM (6 minor), 3 STILL FIX | C1-C25 (23 required, 2 optional), log in `fixes_supertraining_ch4-2a_applied.md` | **passes** |
| *Supertraining* 4.2b (4.2.4-4.2.9) | 20 | round-1 fixes by a separate fixer, then `review_supertraining_ch4-2b_opus_round2.md`: 14 FIXED, 1 GO, 3 STILL FIX, 2 NEW PROBLEM | C1-C9 (all required), log in `fixes_supertraining_ch4-2b_applied.md` | **passes** |

In every batch, the round-2 reviewer was a different agent from the fixer, and the orchestrator applied the reviewer's corrections verbatim. Each correction's Old string matched exactly once. No reviewer asked for a third round.

Lint after the fixes: Zatsiorsky 0 issues. Issurin 3, all known false positives (the `_book.md` dashes and the two wrapped headers in Ch3). Supertraining 1, the known `_book.md` false positive.

**Promotion dry run** (`python scripts/promote_to_vault.py strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky strength-and-conditioning/block-periodization--issurin strength-and-conditioning/science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky`):
- *Supertraining*: 41 new, 1 changed (`_book.md`), 0 vault-only.
- Issurin: 10 new, 1 changed (`_book.md`), 0 vault-only.
- Zatsiorsky: 18 new (17 entries + `_book.md`), 0 changed.
- Unresolved links: 0.

The only "changed" files are the two `_book.md`s, as expected.

**Other outputs**
- **Reciprocal links:** `staging/reciprocal_links_2026-09-28.md` has 42 rows, 3 dropped and 2 manual edits (a text replacement in the vault Ch3 natural-asymmetry entry, and dropping "unverified" in the Evans overload entry). Every target is in the three folders being promoted, so the file only applies after promotion.
- **`_domain.md` merge text:** `staging/_domain_merge_sc_2026-09-28.md` adds Zatsiorsky and updates the Supertraining and Issurin counts.
- **CVASPS:** `docs/cvasps-corroboration-proposals.md`.
  - ASR spot-check: 5 passages checked and 47 suspect spots flagged. Stage 1 of the gate is **not** complete: someone has to listen to the flagged spots.
  - 18 of the 34 Evans entries match the talk. 4 are proposed for untested -> supported.
  - 5 entries are qualified by the talk (HRV use, DEXA, the week-4 connector, the fitness-fatigue model).
  - 16 new ideas are listed, each with a timestamp.
  - Proposals only: the Evans entries were not edited.

## Decisions (with reasons)
- **Depth-jump entry is `supported`, not `contested`.** The 4.2a reviewer overruled the fixer. The p.222 contradiction concerns only what happens past the optimum, and it does not dispute the claim in the title.
- **Thrown-load entry stays `contested`, retitled.** Its text contradicts its own Fig 4.8a.
- **Regime-choice entry is `contested`.** The authors write "premature" on p.231 and "reasonable certainty" on p.237.
- **Quad:hamstring ratio entry stays `supported`.** Both book statements fit its claim, and the library has no H:Q source that disagrees.
- **Citations:** Gregory & Bickel 2005 was confirmed on PubMed (Phys Ther 85(4):358-64) and kept. Wilke 1999, Alfredson 1998 and Ward & Shkuratova 2002 were not inserted, because none could be confirmed.
- **Vault write not run.** The task said Eric approves vault writes himself. A later relayed message said he had pre-approved it, but an approval relayed by an agent is not his own. The reciprocal-links dry run, which reads the vault, was also refused by the permission classifier.

## To do next (Eric, or a session he approves)
1. `python scripts/promote_to_vault.py strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky strength-and-conditioning/block-periodization--issurin strength-and-conditioning/science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky --apply`
2. Merge `_domain.md` by hand from `staging/_domain_merge_sc_2026-09-28.md`.
3. `python scripts/apply_reciprocal_links.py staging/reciprocal_links_2026-09-28.md`: run the dry run, then `--apply`, then the dry run again (expect 0 to add). Make the 2 manual edits listed in that file.
4. SecondBrain: `git pull`, `git add Knowledge/library`, commit `ingest(flint 2026-09-28): ...`, `git push`.
5. `memsearch index` on the library, then spot-check one new Zatsiorsky entry.
6. `python scripts/sync_back_from_vault.py` on the three folders. A promote dry run should then show 0 new and 0 changed. Commit in Flint.
7. After the Evans vault edits in step 3, sync the Evans staging copies too, so they match the vault.

## Next after that
- CVASPS: listen to the flagged spots (or check them against captions). Then apply the corroboration proposals to the Evans entries and atomize the new ideas.
- Resume points:
  - *Supertraining* 4.3 (printed 241, PDF idx 252).
  - Zatsiorsky Ch3 (printed 47, PDF 56).
  - Bondarchuk Vol I Ch3.
  - CFTS: quote only from page images.
- Missing ideas the reviewers logged:
  - Static vs dynamic contraction differ in the nervous system (Supertraining, PDF 239 / p.228).
  - Issurin Table 4.1, Gould's champion traits, family history.
- Peaking synthesis rev 2 is still waiting on Eric's six questions.
